reason: We have 15 highly auditable, cross-verified claims detailing Masabumi Hosono's background, survival, and subsequent public shaming.
story: Masabumi Hosono, a Japanese railway official, was the only Japanese passenger aboard the RMS Titanic when it struck an iceberg in April 1912. Traveling in second class, Hosono initially resigned himself to death. However, when an officer preparing a lifeboat announced there was room for more, Hosono seized the chance and jumped in. After his rescue by the RMS Carpathia, he recorded his harrowing experience on Titanic stationery—the only known survivor account written on the ship's letterhead. But his survival came at a terrible price. Upon returning to Japan, he was met with severe public condemnation, accused of cowardice, and sacked from his government job for failing to die honorably. Hosono lived out his remaining decades in quiet shame until his death in 1939. Decades later, his descendants published his letter, restoring his honor and proving he did not dishonorably displace others.
angle: The only Japanese passenger to survive the Titanic was publicly shamed and fired from his job because he chose to live rather than die honorably with the ship.

disputed: The exact lifeboat assignment (S1 and S4 place him on Lifeboat 10, but S2 warns that the assignment is probable and should remain qualified).
The claim that Japanese school textbooks cited Hosono as an example of shameful behavior (S1 and S4 report this, but S1 and S2 highlight that a 2007 reinvestigation found no such textbooks).
The claim that he permanently lost his government career (S3 says he lost his job in 1914, but S1 and S2 clarify that he was quickly reemployed and worked until his death).
His age during the disaster (S3 says 42, S4 says 41).
The rumor that he disguised himself as a woman to board the lifeboat (S1 mentions this accusation at a US inquiry, but S2 states there is no reliable evidence he did so).
